metadata.title: What Nurses See Before The End
metadata.description: Hospice nurses often notice certain changes as a person’s final days approach. Discover 70 physical, emotional and practical changes families may see.

landing.title: What Nurses See Before The End
landing.intro: Hospice nurses recognise subtle signs before death that most families miss. Here's what to look for.
landing.adNote: One short ad, then enter the gallery.

introduction: Hospice nurses often notice certain changes as a person's final days approach. Some are surprisingly easy to overlook. Discover what they may mean.
gallery.completeCopy: No single change can predict an exact timeline. A person’s care team can explain what is happening and help protect comfort, dignity and choice.

items.title: Appetite Begins to Fade

image.alt: Illustration of appetite naturally declines

paragraphs: Food and drink may become less appealing as someone grows weaker. This can be difficult for families to watch. Offer what the person wants and can safely manage, and ask the care team how to keep eating and drinking comfortable.

items.title: More Time Spent Resting

image.alt: Illustration of longer periods of rest and sleep

paragraphs: A person may sleep for longer stretches and have less energy for visitors. Short, quiet visits can be easier than lengthy conversations. Follow their lead and allow plenty of rest without assuming that sleep alone reveals how much time remains.

items.title: Breathing Changes Its Rhythm

image.alt: Illustration of breathing becomes uneven

paragraphs: Breaths may alternate between deeper breathing and pauses, sometimes in a pattern called Cheyne–Stokes breathing. These changes can be unsettling to watch. The care team can explain what is happening and assess whether the person appears uncomfortable.

items.title: Hands and Feet Become Cooler

image.alt: Illustration of extremities feel cooler

paragraphs: Reduced circulation can make hands and feet feel cool, even in a warm room. A light blanket may help with comfort. Ask the nurse before using heating pads or hot-water bottles, which can damage fragile skin.

items.title: The Skin Looks Different

image.alt: Illustration of changes in skin appearance

paragraphs: Skin may become patchy or mottled as circulation changes, particularly on the limbs. The appearance varies with skin tone. Nurses consider these changes alongside other symptoms rather than treating any single skin change as a precise countdown.

items.title: A Noticeable Chill in Fingers and Toes

image.alt: Illustration of chill at the hands and feet

paragraphs: Family members may notice that a loved one’s fingers or toes feel colder than before. Gentle coverings and a comfortable room can help. Let the care team know about new discomfort or unusual changes so they can assess them.

items.title: The Pulse Becomes Harder to Feel

image.alt: Illustration of fading heartbeat signal

paragraphs: A person’s pulse can become weaker or change its rhythm near the end of life. This is one part of the overall picture nurses assess. Families do not need to keep checking it; being present can be more helpful.

items.title: Temperature Becomes Less Predictable

image.alt: Illustration of unsteady internal temperature

paragraphs: Someone may feel warm one moment and cool the next. Adjust bedding gently to their comfort rather than piling on heavy covers. Tell the care team about fever, shaking or distress, because some causes can still be treated.

items.title: Small, Unexpected Muscle Jerks

image.alt: Illustration of brief random muscle movements

paragraphs: Brief twitches or jerks may occur during serious illness. Medicines and changes in the body can contribute. These movements do not automatically mean pain, but new or repeated jerking should be mentioned to the nurse for assessment.

items.title: Swallowing Becomes More Difficult

image.alt: Illustration of trouble with swallowing

paragraphs: Weakness can make food, drinks and tablets harder to swallow. Do not push meals or sips if the person coughs or struggles. The nurse can advise on mouth care, safer comfort measures and other ways to give needed medicines.

items.title: Meals Lose Their Appeal

image.alt: Illustration of reduced interest in eating

paragraphs: Favourite foods may no longer tempt someone who is very unwell. Offer small amounts if wanted and safe to swallow, without pressure to finish. The goal is comfort and enjoyment, with the care team guiding any concerns about intake.

items.title: Less Urine Is Passed

image.alt: Illustration of less frequent urine production

paragraphs: Urine may become darker or less frequent as intake and kidney function change. This does not, by itself, decide whether fluids are needed. Let the nurse know about pain, a swollen lower abdomen or difficulty passing urine.

items.title: Restlessness Replaces Stillness

image.alt: Illustration of increased restlessness and pacing

paragraphs: Some people become restless, fidget repeatedly or try to get out of bed. Pain, constipation, a full bladder or medicines may contribute. A calm setting helps, but the care team should also look for causes that can be relieved.

items.title: Familiar Surroundings Become Confusing

image.alt: Illustration of moments of confusion and losing bearings

paragraphs: A person may lose track of where they are or who is nearby. Speak calmly, introduce yourself and offer familiar reassurance. New confusion deserves a clinical review, especially if it is frightening or comes with agitation.

items.title: Longer Periods Without Responding

image.alt: Illustration of long stretches of deep sleep

paragraphs: Someone may become harder to wake and eventually stop responding. This is different from ordinary restorative sleep. Keep speaking gently and let the nurse assess comfort, since a lack of response does not prove that no discomfort is present.

items.title: A Rattling Sound With Breathing

image.alt: Illustration of noisy breathing near the end

paragraphs: Saliva or mucus can collect when a person is too weak to clear it, producing a wet or rattling sound. It can upset listeners without necessarily troubling the person. Nurses may suggest repositioning or other comfort measures.

items.title: Comforting Dreams or Visions

image.alt: Illustration of seeing people or scenes that comfort

paragraphs: Some people describe vivid dreams or seeing familiar people who are not present. Listen without arguing or insisting on an explanation. If the experience becomes frightening or is accompanied by confusion, tell the care team so they can help.

items.title: An Unexpected Moment of Alertness

image.alt: Illustration of a sudden bright moment

paragraphs: Occasionally someone who has been very drowsy becomes briefly more alert or conversational. It can be a welcome chance to connect. Such a change does not reliably predict recovery or the exact timing of death.

items.title: Talking About Letting Go

image.alt: Illustration of a gradual surrendering feeling

paragraphs: Some people express acceptance or say they feel ready to let go. Others remain worried or uncertain, and both responses deserve respect. Listen to what matters to them without expecting a particular emotional or spiritual experience.

items.title: Tiredness Becomes Overwhelming

image.alt: Illustration of progressive deepening tiredness

paragraphs: Profound fatigue can make even simple conversation exhausting. Offer company in manageable moments and avoid expecting the person to stay awake for visitors. Nurses can help families understand changes in energy while continuing to assess comfort.

items.title: A Quieter Connection With Others

image.alt: Illustration of a gentle withdrawal

paragraphs: A person may seem less interested in the room around them or in conversation. This can feel painful for loved ones, but it need not mean rejection. Quiet company and familiar voices can still offer reassurance.

items.title: A Brief Return of Clear Conversation

image.alt: Illustration of a sudden bright moment

paragraphs: A short spell of clearer awareness sometimes follows a period of confusion or sleepiness. Let the person set the pace rather than overwhelming them with questions. These moments vary widely and are not guaranteed to occur.

items.title: Everyday Movements Become Harder

image.alt: Illustration of profound loss of strength

paragraphs: Severe weakness may make turning, sitting up or washing difficult. Offer help that protects dignity, and ask staff about safe movement and positioning. Forcing activity can be tiring; small adjustments may make a greater difference to comfort.

items.title: Warmth or Tingling in One Area

image.alt: Illustration of localized warmth or pins and needles

paragraphs: A person may describe tingling, warmth or other unusual sensations during illness. There can be several causes, so these feelings are not reliable signs that death is imminent. Mention new, painful or persistent sensations to the care team.

items.title: Pressure on Fragile Skin

image.alt: Illustration of skin damage from sustained pressure

paragraphs: Long periods in one position increase the risk of pressure sores. Nurses may use supportive mattresses, skin checks and gentle repositioning to reduce this risk. Report sore, discoloured or broken skin promptly rather than assuming it is unavoidable.

items.title: An Unexpected Sense of Calm

image.alt: Illustration of unexpected serenity

paragraphs: Some people become unusually calm during advanced illness. Others experience changing emotions throughout. Follow the person’s wishes and offer reassurance without suggesting that serenity is something everyone should feel or a sign with a fixed meaning.

items.title: Feeling Light or Floating

image.alt: Illustration of sensation of floating

paragraphs: Some people describe feeling light, floating or detached from their body. Their account may have personal meaning, but it is not a universal experience or a clinical countdown. Listen respectfully and report distressing sensations to the care team.

items.title: Sleepiness Deepens Through the Day

image.alt: Illustration of deepening sleepiness

paragraphs: Frequent dozing can gradually leave fewer moments of wakefulness. Keep the environment restful and speak gently during care. If drowsiness changes suddenly or causes concern, the nurse can consider illness, medicines and other possible contributors.

items.title: A Dry, Uncomfortable Mouth

image.alt: Illustration of mouth dryness

paragraphs: A dry mouth can make speaking and swallowing uncomfortable even when someone does not ask for a drink. Regular mouth care and lip moisturising may help. Ask the nurse what is safe, particularly if the person cannot swallow easily.

items.title: Changes in Vision

image.alt: Illustration of dimming sight

paragraphs: Someone may find it harder to focus or describe a change in what they can see. Keep familiar objects nearby and lighting comfortable. New or sudden visual changes should be assessed; they are not automatically part of dying.

items.title: When Responses to Sound Become Less Clear

image.alt: Illustration of fading ability to hear

paragraphs: A person may no longer respond when spoken to, but this does not necessarily mean they cannot hear. Continue using a calm, familiar voice. Avoid talking about them as though they are absent, even when they cannot answer.

items.title: Touch May Feel Different

image.alt: Illustration of increased sensitivity to contact

paragraphs: Some people welcome a hand to hold, while others find contact uncomfortable. Ask permission when possible and watch their response. Gentle care should follow the person’s preferences rather than assuming that every touch will feel soothing.

items.title: Nausea Needs Attention

image.alt: Illustration of rising queasiness and vomiting risk

paragraphs: Queasiness or vomiting can make a difficult time more uncomfortable. Illness, medicines and other problems may contribute. Tell the care team so they can assess the cause and offer relief instead of treating nausea as something to endure.

items.title: Twitching or Spasms Under the Skin

image.alt: Illustration of uncontrolled muscle movements

paragraphs: Muscle movements may be visible even when a person is resting. Their cause can include medicine effects or changes in body chemistry. Let the nurse know if they are new, frequent or seem distressing so care can be reviewed.

items.title: Breaths Become Quieter or Shallower

image.alt: Illustration of softening of the breath

paragraphs: Breathing may become softer and less regular as a person grows weaker. Watch for signs of distress rather than judging comfort from the sound alone. The nurse can explain changes and help if breathing appears difficult.

items.title: Swelling From Fluid Build-Up

image.alt: Illustration of accumulating fluid in tissues

paragraphs: Fluid can collect in the tissues during advanced illness, causing swollen hands, feet or other areas. It may have several causes. Let the team assess new swelling, discomfort or coughing, particularly when breathing is affected.

items.title: Circulation Changes in the Limbs

image.alt: Illustration of slowing circulation in limbs

paragraphs: Coolness and changes in skin colour may develop as circulation becomes poorer. Keep the person comfortably covered and handle fragile skin gently. Nurses assess the wider situation, including whether there is pain or another problem needing attention.

items.title: Pressure or Tightness in the Chest

image.alt: Illustration of sensation of tightness in the body

paragraphs: Chest pressure or tightness should not simply be dismissed as a normal part of dying. Tell the care team promptly so they can assess and relieve it. For sudden severe symptoms without an established care plan, seek urgent medical help.

items.title: Skin Becomes Damp or Clammy

image.alt: Illustration of skin feeling moist or clammy

paragraphs: Sweating or clammy skin may accompany illness, medicines or temperature changes. Dry bedding and gentle washing can improve comfort. Let the nurse know about new sweating, fever or distress so the cause can be considered.

items.title: Energy for Interaction Fades

image.alt: Illustration of deepening exhaustion and sleepiness

paragraphs: Longer sleep and shorter conversations may reflect growing exhaustion. There is no need to fill every silence or wake someone for every visitor. Brief, peaceful company can be enough, with staff helping to monitor comfort.

items.title: Aches and Soreness Need Relief

image.alt: Illustration of late stage body soreness

paragraphs: Pain may appear as aching, pressure or discomfort during movement. It can often be eased with an individual care plan. Mention grimacing, groaning or guarding a painful area, especially if the person cannot explain what they feel.

items.title: Food Becomes Harder to Tolerate

image.alt: Illustration of gradual decline of digestion

paragraphs: Advanced illness can change appetite and digestion, making meals less comfortable. Offer small amounts only if wanted and safe. Tell the nurse about constipation, nausea or abdominal pain, because these symptoms may still be relieved.

items.title: The Feeling of Not Getting Enough Air

image.alt: Illustration of trouble getting enough air

paragraphs: Breathlessness can be frightening and deserves prompt attention. Repositioning and prescribed treatments may help, depending on the cause and care plan. Tell the team about distress; oxygen is not automatically the right treatment for everyone.

items.title: A Tight or Uncomfortable Throat

image.alt: Illustration of sensation of throat tightness

paragraphs: Difficulty swallowing or a tight throat needs assessment, particularly if breathing is affected. Do not force food, drinks or tablets. The nurse can suggest safe comfort measures and review symptoms and medicines with the clinical team.

items.title: Favourite Flavours Taste Different

image.alt: Illustration of changes in flavor perception

paragraphs: Illness, treatments and a dry mouth may change how food tastes. If the person wants to eat and can swallow safely, small tastes of favourite foods may be welcome. There is no need to insist when eating becomes unpleasant.

items.title: Movement Gives Way to Stillness

image.alt: Illustration of muscles easing into stillness

paragraphs: Someone may move less as strength and responsiveness decline. Stillness does not automatically mean comfort or the absence of pain. Staff continue checking for signs of distress and may gently adjust positioning to support the body.

items.title: Breathing Becomes Light and Irregular

image.alt: Illustration of breathing becoming light and uneven

paragraphs: Shallow breaths and uneven pauses can occur near the end of life. They may look unfamiliar to family members. Ask the nurse to explain the pattern and assess comfort rather than trying to interpret each breath yourself.

items.title: The Heartbeat Changes Its Pattern

image.alt: Illustration of heartbeat shifting in unpredictable ways

paragraphs: The pulse may become weaker, faster, slower or less regular during decline. Nurses consider it with the person’s other symptoms. A pulse change alone cannot tell a family exactly when death will happen.

items.title: Cool Limbs and Patchy Colour

image.alt: Illustration of extremities cooling as circulation changes

paragraphs: Hands and feet may cool alongside changes in skin colour. Gentle coverings can help maintain comfort, and the nurse can explain what they observe. Avoid strong heat directly against the skin, especially when sensation is reduced.

items.title: Feeling Distant From the Surroundings

image.alt: Illustration of sensation of lightness and detachment

paragraphs: Some people describe drifting or feeling detached from the room around them. Listen to their description without imposing a spiritual or medical explanation. If it is frightening or sudden, let the care team assess what may be contributing.

items.title: Conversation Becomes Less Frequent

image.alt: Illustration of gentle withdrawal from conversation

paragraphs: A person may speak less because of fatigue, weakness or changing awareness. Respect quiet moments and keep communication simple. Being nearby can still matter, even when there is little conversation or no response.

items.title: Acceptance Can Take Different Forms

image.alt: Illustration of a calm acceptance settles in

paragraphs: Some people speak openly and calmly about the end of life; others prefer not to. Neither response is a measure of how well they are coping. Offer space for their feelings and ask what support they would find helpful.

items.title: Less Interest in Food and Drinks

image.alt: Illustration of reduced interest in eating and drinking

paragraphs: Reduced intake is common as someone becomes very unwell, but care should remain individual. Offer safe sips or small tastes if wanted. Mouth care can help with dryness, and fluid decisions should be discussed with the clinical team.

items.title: Stiffness Makes Repositioning Difficult

image.alt: Illustration of increasing body stiffness and strain

paragraphs: Immobility or illness can leave a person feeling stiff or tense. Slow, supported repositioning may help, guided by staff. Tell the nurse about painful movement so the care plan can protect comfort rather than forcing the body to move.

items.title: Breathing Changes From Moment to Moment

image.alt: Illustration of fluctuating breathing patterns

paragraphs: Breathing may alternate between quiet periods and more noticeable effort. Report signs of breathlessness or anxiety so the team can respond. A calm room can help, but it does not replace assessment and treatment when needed.

items.title: Less Visible Reaction to Pain

image.alt: Illustration of dulled pain responses near the end

paragraphs: Someone who is less responsive may show fewer outward reactions even when discomfort is present. Do not assume that pain has disappeared. Nurses look for non-verbal signs and continue reviewing symptom relief as awareness changes.

items.title: Familiar Carers Become a Source of Comfort

image.alt: Illustration of deepening emotional connections with care staff

paragraphs: A familiar nurse or carer may offer reassurance during a vulnerable time. Some people express gratitude or welcome their presence; others prefer family or quiet. Respect individual wishes and the relationships that help the person feel secure.

items.title: Shivers or Tremors Appear

image.alt: Illustration of intermittent shivers and muscle tremors

paragraphs: Shaking may reflect temperature changes, medicines or other causes. A comfortable covering can help if the person feels cold. Tell the nurse about new or persistent tremors, especially with fever or distress, so the cause can be assessed.

items.title: Putting Personal Belongings in Order

image.alt: Illustration of need to sort personal items and space

paragraphs: Some people want to arrange possessions, give items away or organise their surroundings. This can be a meaningful choice rather than a medical sign. Offer practical help without taking control or pressuring them to finish everything.

items.title: The Gaze and Blinking Change

image.alt: Illustration of subtle changes in eye activity

paragraphs: Eyes may stay partly open, blink less or seem less focused as responsiveness changes. Staff can advise on eye comfort and care. These observations do not reveal what someone is thinking or provide proof of a spiritual experience.

items.title: Humour Still Finds a Place

image.alt: Illustration of quiet playfulness

paragraphs: Gentle jokes or familiar humour may remain part of a person’s personality during serious illness. Follow their lead and enjoy these moments if they welcome them. Humour can offer connection without denying the seriousness of the situation.

items.title: Reflecting on Who They Have Been

image.alt: Illustration of shifts in how people see themselves

paragraphs: Illness can prompt reflection on identity, relationships and the roles someone has held. Listen without rushing to provide answers. A person may value being recognised for their life and interests, not only for the care they now need.

items.title: Wanting the Comfort of Familiar Places

image.alt: Illustration of longing for known places

paragraphs: Someone may express a wish to be at home or near treasured surroundings. Ask what those places mean to them and discuss achievable options with the team. Familiar photos, music or belongings may help when a move is not possible.

items.title: Speaking About Unfinished Matters

image.alt: Illustration of voicing regrets and loose ends

paragraphs: Regrets or unresolved relationships may become important topics. Listen without promising that everything can be fixed. If the person wishes, help arrange a conversation or seek support from a counsellor, chaplain or another trusted professional.

items.title: Sharing Stories and Life Lessons

image.alt: Illustration of passing along life lessons

paragraphs: A person may want to pass on advice, memories or family stories. Let them choose what to share and whether to record it. These conversations can create a valued keepsake, but no one should feel pressured to produce a final message.

items.title: Hair and Nails Become More Fragile

image.alt: Illustration of thinning and weakening of hair and nails

paragraphs: Long illness, nutrition changes and some treatments can affect hair and nails. These changes are not reliable signs that death is close. Gentle grooming may support dignity and comfort, with care tailored to the person’s wishes.

items.title: Small Temperature Changes Feel Uncomfortable

image.alt: Illustration of increased sensitivity to hot and cold

paragraphs: Someone who is frail may feel uncomfortable when the room becomes warmer or cooler. Adjust covers and ventilation gradually, following their preferences. Ask the nurse about fever or persistent chills rather than assuming all temperature changes are expected.

items.title: Secretions Make Breathing Sound Noisy

image.alt: Illustration of noisy breathing from throat secretions

paragraphs: A person who can no longer clear saliva or mucus may make a gurgling sound with each breath. The sound can worry relatives. Nurses can explain it and consider positioning or treatment, while checking for any signs of distress.

items.title: Vivid Images or Memories Hold Their Attention

image.alt: Illustration of concentrated visual awareness and imagery

paragraphs: Some people describe powerful memories, dreamlike scenes or images others cannot see. Listen respectfully to the meaning they give them. Distressing experiences or new confusion should be raised with staff rather than assumed to be comforting.

items.title: Closeness With Family Remains Meaningful

image.alt: Illustration of tender physical connections with family

paragraphs: Holding hands, sitting nearby or a gentle embrace may offer connection when words are difficult. Follow the person’s wishes and comfort, since touch is not always welcome. Quiet presence can be just as meaningful as a conversation.
